items.body: `spaceStatus` only recognizes directly impossible individual setup constraints. Provably empty combinations—such as `actionsExactly := [A]` plus `sequence [B]`, a positive bound on a disallowed action, conflicting setup constraints, or an exact trace violating ordering—are returned as `.satisfiable` even though `admits` rejects every trace. Downstream queries can therefore misreport an empty behavior instead of `unsatisfiable`.
items.suggestion: Add cross-constraint satisfiability checking, including setup equivalence/difference closure and validation of exact schedules/traces against sequence, adjacency, ordering, bounds, allow/forbid, and setup constraints. If general satisfiability remains planner-owned, avoid asserting `.satisfiable` until that determination is available.
items.title: `spaceStatus` only recognizes directly impossible individual setup constraints

items.body: Canonical setup projection preserves `left`/`right` operand order even though both implemented relations, `equal` and `different`, are symmetric. Swapping operands leaves membership unchanged but changes canonical bytes and `semanticDigest`, violating source-order independence for semantically unordered data.
items.suggestion: Canonically order the two operands for symmetric relations before storing or projecting each setup constraint, and add a digest-equivalence test for operand reversal.

items.body: `hasOccurrenceAssignment` exhaustively tries every unused schedule position and checks ordering only after assigning all occurrences. An ordinary non-matching candidate—such as 14 matching positions for 15 required occurrences—can explore roughly `14!` assignments before returning false, creating a straightforward CPU/resource-exhaustion path.
items.suggestion: Reject per-action count deficits before assignment, prune partial assignments against ordering constraints, and use a memoized or grouped matching algorithm so bounded malformed/non-member candidates cannot trigger factorial work.
items.title: `hasOccurrenceAssignment` exhaustively tries every unused schedule position and checks ordering only after assigning all occurrences

items.body: The replacement occurrence algorithm removes factorial permutation duplication but still materializes exponentially many states. With `n` unordered required occurrences sharing one action and `n` matching schedule positions, the fold retains every remaining-occurrence subset—up to `2^n` lists—before testing for an empty state. Thus the original memory/CPU exhaustion path remains.
items.suggestion: Add an explicit occurrence-state budget or authoring bound and fail closed when exceeded. Preferably, prune dominated states or use a matching algorithm that does not retain every subset; short-circuit once a successful empty state becomes reachable.
